p.x:
How You Can Build Software That is Orders of Magnitude Faster On Today’s Hardware

Over the years hardware has kept getting faster, but our daily experience using software has not. The tools we use to get our job done daily often are excruciatingly slow, sucking a lot of joy out of our work. Let’s take a look at how today’s hardware is massively underutilized and just how much faster things could be.

First, let’s take a look at what a computer fundamentally does. It manipulates memory using one or more CPU cores that execute instructions at a number of cycles per second. Reading and writing from memory is expensive. How expensive depends on whether you’re reading from the L1 cache in a core (around 3-4 cycles), any of the other caches mostly shared between cores (L2 around 10-12 cycles, L3 around 30-70 cycles), or the RAM memory (100-150 cycles).

This means we have a few levers we can play with:

• Execute less instructions to get the same work done. When using an interpreted language, a lot of extra work needs to be done to execute your code. While an “add” may be one CPU instruction, an interpreted language needs to figure out all kinds of things before it can actually execute that “add”. Multiply this by many lines of code and amount of wasted instructions is tremendous. Depending on whether an interpreted languages uses a JIT compilar and whether the JIT correctly optimizes your code, you can gain more than 10x-100x speed improvements by using a lower level language just because you’re executing less instructions. I can’t recommed Casey Muratori’s Performance-Aware Programming course [1] enough where he begins by demonstrating all the things Python is doing to execute a simple addition.

• Reduce the amount of cache misses. By adopting simpler programming practices, you can learn to lay out the data of your program in such a way that less of it is accessed at the time and more fits in faster caches. This includes things like splitting your structs so they only contain data needed by use case, using smaller data types, using simple arrays of structs where possible instead of more complex structures, etc. This can easily get you another 20x speedup, which combined with the previous point gives us a 200x-2000x speedup. To learn more, I recommend starting with Mike Acton’s [2] and Andrew Kelly’s [3] talks about Data-Oriented Design.

• Use mutliple cores. As things are now, it looks like individual CPU cores are not getting much faster. So we’re getting more CPU cores instead, which you can’t use if you’re not multi-threading. This doesn’t only give you a speed boost because you can execute more instructions per second, but also each CPU has its own L1 cache, multiplying the amount of L1 cache by the number of cores in your machine! This can again speed up our programs by at least 4x on a quad core if done correctly.

All these things together can give us 800x-8000x speedup already, not even covering SIMD! What can you do with this extra speed? First of all, we should expect all software to be instant. Second, if our programs are faster, we can do more useful work creating entirely new experiences and tools. But if these possibilities are just waiting out there, why aren’t we using them? I think it all starts with assumed beliefs about trade-offs in developer productivity and performance, along with a lack of knowledge how fast our computers are and the history of computing. The good news is that writing performant code is simpler than you think. But that’s a topic for another post  :)

Currently, I’m exploring low-level programming using Zig to build a software architecture visualization tool. I’m writing it in the simplest, most naive way using only GLFW and OpenGL, only adding complexity where needed. I wrote a YAML and Typescript parser from scratch, with only the features I need so I can reduce problems which could be quite complex down to something manageable to quickly experiment with. This project is my personal playground in trade-offs, programming techniques and performance investigation. If that sounds interesting, stay in touch!

p.x:
🚨 BREAKING: Former President of Russian Republic Claims He Was Contacted By Aliens And Invited Onboard A UFO While In Office 🚨

Kirsan Ilyumzhinov, former President of the Republic of Kalmykia and longtime President of the World Chess Federation (FIDE), gives the most detailed public account to date of an alleged extraterrestrial encounter that occurred while he was a sitting head of state in September 1997. He also makes extraordinary claims about UFO knowledge shared among specific world leaders, intelligence agencies, and religious institutions.

Ilyumzinov held senior political office, sat in Russia’s State Council, advised Vladimir Putin, met repeatedly with Henry Kissinger, Jimmy Carter, Pope John Paul II, and is close friends with the Dalai Lama. He says his UFO experience was acknowledged by Boris Yeltsin and discussed with Putin. He also mentioned having a deep discussion about it with Henry Kissinger who seemed to know all about UFOs before speaking with him.

Key points from the episode:

1. The 1997 Encounter (Moscow):
While on an official trip to Moscow, Ilyumzhinov says he was “invited” into a glowing, translucent tube from his penthouse apartment and transported to a large craft. He describes a vast interior space, multiple humanoid beings wearing yellow garments, and telepathic communication. He emphasizes he was calm, conscious, and sober and spent hours onboard the ship talking to the beings.

2. Independent Witnesses:
His chief of staff, driver, and a minister arrived at his apartment the next morning to escort him to the airport. They searched the apartment for over an hour. Phones, clothes, shoes were untouched. No exit recorded. He then appeared suddenly from a room they had already searched multiple times. Police were contacted at the time.

3. The Message Conveyed:
The beings told him humanity was still at an “embryonic” stage of development  technologically advanced but spiritually immature. They criticized war, environmental destruction, and weapons development, comparing humanity’s behavior to ants destroying their own nest.

4. Telepathic Communication:
Ilyumzhinov says the beings did not speak aloud. Communication occurred “through thoughts,” similar to descriptions he later heard from mystic Baba Vanga. He likens the experience to non-verbal information transfer rather than language.

5. Cold War UFO Knowledge:
He recounts being told by Mikhail Gorbachev about a private meeting between Nixon and Brezhnev where a small classified folder was shown. According to Gorbachev, after that meeting, both U.S. and Soviet lunar programs abruptly halted despite ongoing missions being prepared.

6. Kissinger’s Awareness:
Ilyumzinov describes multiple meetings with Henry Kissinger, including private conversations with Kissinger and Gorbachev present. He claims Kissinger demonstrated detailed familiarity with UFO knowledge held by U.S. agencies, asking technical questions rather than expressing disbelief.

7. Putin and Yeltsin:
He says Boris Yeltsin privately acknowledges awareness of the incident and asked whether Ilyumzhinov felt mentally well or was drunk. Putin later asked him directly to recount the event in detail, including whether he had been drinking. Ilyumzhinov insists he told the truth despite political risk.

8. Other World Leaders:
He claims a close friend who was a sitting president of a large country privately told him he had seen a UFO and met alien beings while on a fishing trip but didn’t want to disclose this to the public for fear of ridicule.

9. The Vatican and the Dalai Lama:
Ilyumzhinov states Pope John Paul II said “we are not alone” and references a Vatican observatory tasked with studying extraterrestrial phenomena. He says the Dalai Lama expressed similar views, framing non-human intelligence as part of a broader metaphysics.

10. Underground and Underwater Civilizations
He claims military forces from multiple nations detected unidentified craft underwater during the Cold War, prompting covert coordination to avoid nuclear escalation. He also asserts underground civilizations exist, referencing folklore, geological anomalies, and his friend Bulgarian Mystic Baba Vanga’s statements.

11. Why He Spoke Out:
Ilyumzhinov says he waited months before going public due to political consequences. He ultimately decided someone in power had to speak first, or the subject would remain stigmatized forever.

12. The Broader Claim:
He believes non-human intelligence is slowly creating a “critical mass” of human awareness by contacting individuals across society, politicians, scientists, mystics, and civilians, to prepare humanity for eventual open contact.

If a former head of state with access to intelligence briefings, world leaders, and religious authorities says this happened, and multiple witnesses confirm unexplained disappearance, the question is no longer whether the story is strange...the question is why it has been ignored.

Full Documentary 👇

p.x:
I quit weed two weeks ago.

The reason it was such a treacherous drug, at least for me, was that it never really became a problem. I never got bad grades, lost a job, or messed up a relationship due to it. There was never a point where I hit rock bottom, where I was sucking dick in some back alley to afford the next joint; there was never a come-to-Jesus moment.

It was just a bad habit, one that had been causing me to operate at ~85% capacity for years and years. So I decided to quit. Unfortunately, this meant dealing with withdrawal.

I think the popular opinion of weed is that its withdrawal symptoms lie somewhere between "mild" and "nonexistent." That wasn't the case for me. I'll grant that weed withdrawal is, I assume, not as bad as withdrawal from other drugs. But for me, it absolutely sucked.

If you weren't aware, the withdrawal symptoms for weed almost perfectly mirror the symptoms of smoking it. Whereas smoking makes you sleepy, quitting gives you insomnia. Whereas smoking makes you hungry, quitting makes you lose your appetite. And whereas smoking makes you euphoric, quitting makes you grumpy and depressed.

For me, these depressed feelings were especially bad.

While I was quitting, I was furious and miserable all the time. I despised the world and everyone in it. And it was so easy for me to rationalize these emotions! I would say that these feelings were the natural response to living in such a shitty world. And only after ranting to myself for three hours would I snap out of it and realize it was the withdrawal talking.

That's what inspired the quoted post about the New Mexican Cube. You think that you're depressed because the world sucks, but actually, you think the world sucks because you're depressed. Emotions don't necessarily follow from your perceptions; often they precede them.

(I felt kind of bad about the post anyway, since it seemed like some people were actually planning to go to that location. While going to the cube would certainly make them angry, it wouldn't be for the reasons they thought!)

Anyway, this is your sign to quit whatever terrible habit you have. The basil bush in my garden burst aflame and God told me to make this post, just for you. He says you ignored the two boats he sent, and hopes that you won't overlook this helicopter as well.
